extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates, graduate students, and researchers in functional analysis/convex analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Textbook chapter material giving definitions, geometric forms of the Hahn–Banach theorem, properties of gauges and hyperplanes, duality and conjugation for convex functions, and Fenchel–Moreau / Fenchel–Rockafellar duality results. Useful for proving separation results, constructing supporting functionals, and applying convex duality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine hyperplane: definition and closedness criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: An affine hyperplane is a subset H = {x ∈ E ; f(x) = α} where f is a linear functional that does not vanish identically and α ∈ R. Proposition 1.5: H = [f = α] is closed if and only if f is continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric interpretation: H is an equation f = α. Proof sketch: continuity ⇒ H closed. Conversely, if H closed pick x0 in complement, obtain a ball around x0 contained in complement, deduce a uniform bound on f on that ball giving continuity and a bound on ||f||.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation and strict separation by a hyperplane
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyperplane H = [f = α] separates A and B if f(x) ≤ α for all x ∈ A and f(x) ≥ α for all y ∈ B. H strictly separates A and B if there exists ε > 0 such that f(x) ≤ α − ε on A and f(x) ≥ α + ε on B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric meaning: A and B lie in disjoint closed half-spaces determined by H. Strict separation requires a uniform gap ε between the images of A and B under f.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hahn–Banach, first geometric form (Theorem 1.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A and B are two nonempty convex subsets of E with A ∩ B = ∅ and at least one of them is open, then there exists a closed hyperplane that separates A and B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Minkowski functional (gauge) of C = A − B and extends a functional from the line through a point via algebraic Hahn–Banach to produce a separating functional f. Applicable whenever one set is open; no compactness or closedness assumption needed for mere separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minkowski functional (gauge) p and its properties (Lemma 1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an open convex set C with 0 ∈ C, define p(x) = inf{α > 0; α^{-1}x ∈ C}. Then p satisfies sublinearity and homogeneity properties (the text refers to (1) and (2)), there exists M with 0 ≤ p(x) ≤ M||x||, and C = {x ∈ E ; p(x) < 1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: p is used to control linear functionals and to build extensions: one shows upper bounds on p via a ball contained in C, convexity gives p(x+y) ≤ p(x)+p(y) (up to ε), and openness gives the characterization C = {p < 1}. p is central to constructing supporting functionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supporting functional separating a point and an open convex set (Lemma 1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If C ⊂ E is nonempty, open, convex and x0 ∉ C, then there exists f ∈ E* such that f(x) < f(x0) for every x ∈ C. In particular the hyperplane [f = f(x0)] separates {x0} and C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: translate so 0 ∈ C, use the gauge p of C, define g on the line Rx0 by g(tx0)=t and show g ≤ p on that line, then apply algebraic Hahn–Banach (Theorem 1.1) to extend g to E with f ≤ p, producing the desired strict inequality on C. Ensures existence of a continuous separating functional when one set is a single point outside an open convex set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hahn–Banach, second geometric form (Theorem 1.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A and B are nonempty convex subsets with A ∩ B = ∅, and A is closed while B is compact, then there exists a closed hyperplane that strictly separates A and B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces to separation of a compact ball and a closed convex set using the first geometric form, then produces a strict gap ε > 0 and chooses α between sup_A f and inf_B f to obtain strict separation. Compactness of one set and closedness of the other give the stronger strict-separation conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of nonzero continuous functional vanishing on a proper subspace (Corollary 1.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F ⊂ E is a linear subspace with F ≠ E, then there exists f ∈ E*, f ≠ 0, such that ⟨f, x⟩ = 0 for all x ∈ F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Theorem 1.7 with A = F (closed linear subspace) and B = {x0} for some x0 ∉ F. The separating hyperplane yields a nonzero functional annihilating F. This fact is often used to prove density: if every continuous linear functional vanishing on F vanishes on E, then F is dense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual, bidual, canonical embedding J and reflexivity criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Given E with dual E*, the bidual E** is the dual of E*. The canonical injection J : E → E** is defined by (Jx)(f) = ⟨f, x⟩. J is linear and an isometry: ||Jx||_{E**} = ||x||_E. E is reflexive iff J is surjective (i.e., E = E**).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identification of E as a subspace of E** via J is standard. Non-surjectivity of J occurs in many Banach spaces; reflexivity is a strong property with many consequences for attainment of suprema and compactness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthogonality relations and bipolar for subspaces (Proposition 1.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a linear subspace M ⊂ E define M^⊥ = {f ∈ E* ; ⟨f,x⟩ = 0 ∀x ∈ M}. For N ⊂ E* define N^⊥ = {x ∈ E ; ⟨f,x⟩ = 0 ∀f ∈ N}. Then (M^⊥)^⊥ = M and (N^⊥)^⊥ ⊃ N. In general (N^⊥)^⊥ may be strictly larger than N.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The equality for M uses separation (Theorem 1.7) to rule out points outside M. The failure of equality for N in general is explained by the fact that the separating functional in E** may not come from E (unless E is reflexive); in fact (N^⊥)^⊥ equals the weak-* closure of N in E*.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower semicontinuity (l.s.c.): definition and equivalent properties
rubrics_metrics.description: A function ϕ : E → (−∞, +∞] is l.s.c. if for every λ ∈ R the level set [ϕ ≤ λ] is closed. Equivalently, epi ϕ is closed in E×R; sequential characterizations hold in metric spaces; sums and supremums of l.s.c. functions are l.s.c.; on compact spaces an l.s.c. function attains its infimum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use level-set or epigraph characterizations when checking l.s.c.; l.s.c. implies lower semicontinuity along sequences (lim inf inequality). The closure of epigraph is a standard criterion used in convex analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convex function: definition and basic implications
rubrics_metrics.description: ϕ : E → (−∞, +∞] is convex if ϕ(tx + (1−t)y) ≤ tϕ(x) + (1−t)ϕ(y) ∀x,y ∈ E, ∀t∈(0,1). Equivalently epi ϕ is convex. If ϕ is convex then each level set [ϕ ≤ λ] is convex, sums and supremums of convex functions are convex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convexity of ϕ is checked by epigraph convexity or Jensen-type inequalities. Note the converse that convex level sets need not imply convexity of the function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convex conjugate (Legendre–Fenchel transform) and Young's inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: For ϕ : E → (−∞,+∞] with nonempty domain define ϕ*(f) = sup_{x∈E} {⟨f,x⟩ − ϕ(x)} for f ∈ E*. Then ϕ* is convex and l.s.c., and Young's inequality holds: ⟨f,x⟩ ≤ ϕ(x) + ϕ*(f) for all x ∈ E, f ∈ E*.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ϕ* is the supremum over affine functions of f; it provides a convex l.s.c. envelope in the dual. Young's inequality is a basic tool to relate primal and dual quantities; many classical inequalities are instances of this relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 1.10: existence of finite conjugates and affine minorants
rubrics_metrics.description: If ϕ is convex, l.s.c., and not identically +∞, then ϕ* is not identically +∞; in particular ϕ is bounded below by an affine continuous function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: separate epi ϕ from a point below ϕ(x0) using Hahn–Banach in E×R to obtain an affine functional (f,k) with k>0, which yields a point in the dual where ϕ* is finite. This yields existence of affine continuous minorants of ϕ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fenchel–Moreau theorem (Theorem 1.11): biconjugation equality
rubrics_metrics.description: If ϕ : E → (−∞,+∞] is convex, l.s.c., and not identically +∞, then the biconjugate ϕ** (restricted to E) equals ϕ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard proof splits the case ϕ ≥ 0 then reduces the general case by subtracting an appropriate affine continuous functional. The result identifies convex l.s.c. functions with their biconjugates and underpins convex duality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fenchel–Rockafellar duality (Theorem 1.12) and constraint qualification
rubrics_metrics.description: Let ϕ, ψ : E → (−∞,+∞] be convex. If there exists x0 ∈ D(ϕ)∩D(ψ) at which ϕ is continuous, then inf_{x∈E}{ϕ(x)+ψ(x)} = max_{f∈E*}{−ϕ*(−f) − ψ*(f)} (the supremum is attained and equals a maximum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The continuity-at-a-point condition is a standard qualification guaranteeing zero duality gap and attainment in the dual. Proof uses geometric separation of epigraph and an application of Hahn–Banach to E×R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual-norm representation and attainment conditions (Corollary 1.4 and remarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: For every x ∈ E, ||x|| = sup_{f ∈ E*, ||f||≤1} |⟨f,x⟩| = max_{f ∈ E*, ||f||≤1} |⟨f,x⟩| when the maximum is achieved. The sup in general need not be achieved; it is achieved for reflexive Banach spaces. James's theorem gives a converse: if every f ∈ E* attains the sup, then E is reflexive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Corollary 1.3 to construct an f0 with ||f0|| = ||x|| and ⟨f0,x⟩ = ||x||^2; divide by ||x|| to get a unit norm functional attaining the supremum when possible. Reflexivity is the key property ensuring attainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duality map F(x): existence, characterization, and uniqueness under strict convexity (Corollary 1.3 / Remark 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each x0 ∈ E there exists f0 ∈ E* such that ||f0|| = ||x0|| and ⟨f0,x0⟩ = ||x0||^2. The (possibly multivalued) duality map F(x0) = {f0 ∈ E*; ||f0|| = ||x0||, ⟨f0,x0⟩ = ||x0||^2}. In general F(x) need not be single-valued, but if E* is strictly convex (e.g., E a Hilbert space or L^p with 1<p<∞) then F(x) is unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: F(x) gives supporting functionals achieving the dual norm equality. Strict convexity of the dual norm yields uniqueness of supporting functional; otherwise F(x) can be a convex closed set. Exercises illustrate nonuniqueness in general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual representation of distance to a convex set and to a subspace (Example 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a nonempty convex K ⊂ E and x0 ∈ E, dist(x0,K) = inf_{x∈K} ||x − x0|| = max_{f∈E*, ||f||≤1}{⟨f,x0⟩ − I_K^*(f)}. In particular, if K = M is a linear subspace then dist(x0,M) = max_{f ∈ M^⊥, ||f||≤1} ⟨f,x0⟩.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an application of Fenchel–Rockafellar duality with ϕ(x)=||x−x0|| and ψ=I_K. It provides a dual (support function) characterization of distances and projections; it can be useful when primal minimizers do not exist while the dual attains a maximum.
